Paper 3: The New Testament, Religion in Relation to Philosophy, Ethics and Morality, Historical Development of Islam (570 CE-661CE). Duration: Three Hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; la question 33 imprime « 25 marks » sans parenthèses.

Sujet scanné de trois pages (page de garde, puis 36 questions en six sections : 2.1 Luke 1-6, 2.2 Fourth Gospel 7-12, 2.3 Acts and 1 Corinthians 13-18, 4.1 Philosophy of Religion 19-24, 4.2 Ethics and Morality 25-30, 6.0 Historical Development of Islam 31-36) : filigranes gcerevision.com / Kawlo ignorés, aucune figure ni carte ; aucune question illisible. Les énoncés sont recopiés tels qu'imprimés, fautes comprises.

Aucun corrigé officiel : réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level. Références bibliques, faits de la Sîra, positions de philosophes et de théologiens cités de mémoire et limités à ce qui est bien établi ; relecture par un spécialiste recommandée avant mise en vente. Neutralité observée envers les traditions chrétienne, musulmane et africaine. Les dates et récits de la période de Médine suivent les sources traditionnelles islamiques (« according to the traditional accounts »), discutées par les historiens.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Examine the factors which affect human responsibility over human acts.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Human responsibility means being answerable for one's acts and open to praise or blame. Aristotle and Aquinas taught that a person is fully responsible only for acts that are voluntary, meaning done with knowledge and with freedom. Several factors can increase, reduce or remove this responsibility.

**1. Knowledge and ignorance.** An act done in ignorance of the circumstances or of the consequences, when the ignorance cannot be avoided, is not fully voluntary. Ignorance that comes from negligence or is deliberately cultivated does not excuse. Aquinas distinguished invincible ignorance, which excuses, from vincible ignorance, which only reduces blame.

**2. Freedom and force.** If a person is physically compelled, for example carried or restrained by another, the act is not theirs. Violence from outside, against the will, removes responsibility. Acts done under threat (duress) are a more complex case: they are chosen, but with reduced freedom, so responsibility is lessened but not always removed.

**3. Fear.** Great fear can disturb judgement and limit freedom, as when a person acts to save their life. Aristotle called such acts "mixed", since they are voluntary in themselves but not what one would choose in other circumstances. Law and morality both give some allowance, though fear does not excuse acts that are always wrong, such as betraying innocent people.

**4. Passion and emotion.** Strong anger, desire or grief can reduce deliberation. Aquinas said that passion that precedes the will lessens the voluntariness of the act, while passion deliberately stirred up does not. Where the person could have restrained themselves, responsibility remains.

**5. Habit and character.** Habits formed by repeated choices make acts easy, but responsibility remains because the habit was developed by free choices. Aristotle said that we are responsible for our characters because we are responsible for the acts that formed them. Addiction raises the difficult question of how far the person can still choose.

**6. Mental and physical condition.** Insanity, severe mental illness, intellectual disability, age and intoxication affect understanding and self-control. Children and the severely ill are not held responsible in the same way as normal adults. Voluntary drunkenness, however, is usually not an excuse, since the person accepted the risk.

**7. Social and environmental conditions.** Upbringing, poverty, peer pressure and culture influence conduct. Sociologists and psychologists stress these factors, and some argue that they limit freedom. Most moral traditions accept that they reduce guilt in some cases but not that they remove all responsibility.

**8. Determinism and free will.** Hard determinists argue that if every act is caused by prior events, no one is responsible. Libertarians and compatibilists reply that a person can still act freely when they act from their own reasons, and that the idea of responsibility would otherwise collapse. Religions generally assume free will, as in the teaching that people will be called to account for their deeds.

**9. Intention and circumstances.** The intention of the agent, the seriousness of the matter and the circumstances of the act affect how much blame applies. An unintended harm is judged differently from a deliberate one.

**Conclusion.** Responsibility depends mainly on knowledge and freedom. Ignorance, force, fear, passion, habit, illness and social pressure may reduce or remove it, but the person remains answerable where they could have known better or acted otherwise.
